'''Harry Curtis Galbreath''' (January 1, 1965 – July 27, 2010) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who played several seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), initially with the [[Miami Dolphins]], and later with the [[Green Bay Packers]] and [[New York Jets]]. The 6-foot 1-inch 295-pound Galbreath attended the [[University of Tennessee]] and starred as an [[offensive guard]] for the Volunteers after graduating in 1983 from [[Clarksville High School (Tennessee)|Clarksville High School]] in [[Clarksville, Tennessee]].<ref>''[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=738&pg=64 1985 University of Tennessee Football Guide] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304022836/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=738&pg=64 |date=March 4, 2016 }}'', University of Tennessee, 1985, p. 64.</ref>

Galbreath played in every game of his four-year career as a Volunteer (1984–87), which included being in the starting lineup his last three years.  Volunteers' coach [[Johnny Majors]] once said that Galbreath was the best run blocker he had ever coached.  On the field, Galbreath was aggressive and fundamentally sound, while off the field he garnered first-team All-SEC and first-team All-American honors as a senior in 1987.<ref name="dies">{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/blog/sec/post/_/id/12150/former-vol-harry-galbreath-dies |title=Former Vol Harry Galbreath dies |author=Chris Low |work=[[ESPN]] |date=July 27, 2010 |access-date=September 13, 2010}}</ref>  He also was awarded the prestigious Jacobs Award, given annually to the SEC's top lineman.  In 1991, Galbreath was honored further for his career in the orange and white by being named to Tennessee's 100 Year All-Time Team.

After graduating in 1988 with a degree in human services, Galbreath was an 8th-round draft pick (212th overall) of the [[Miami Dolphins]] in the [[NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1988 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1988/draft.htm |access-date=2023-09-23 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>  Galbreath was named to the NFL All-Rookie Team in 1988 and played five seasons with the Dolphins before moving on.  Galbreath signed with the [[Green Bay Packers]] after the 1992 season and played three seasons in Wisconsin (1993–95), then headed east to the [[New York Jets]], where he played one more season (1996) before retiring.

Upon his retirement from the [[NFL]], Galbreath was named offensive line coach at [[Austin Peay State University]], where he remained for two years before moving on to a five-year stint in the same capacity at [[Tennessee State University]].  In 2005, he was named offensive line coach at [[Hampton University]]. In 2007, he returned to the Volunteers as an associate in the strength and conditioning program.

Off the field, Galbreath was active with the National Incarcerated Parents and Families Network (NIPFN), a [[non-profit organization]] that provides support and education for families of incarcerated parents.

Galbreath died on July 27, 2010, in Mobile, Alabama.<ref name="dies"/>

'''Harry Vonray Swayne''' (born February 2, 1965) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] with the [[Rutgers Scarlet Knights football|Rutgers Scarlet Knights]]. Swayne was selected by the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] in the seventh round of the [[1987 NFL draft]] with the 190th overall pick.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1987 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1987/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-01 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He is one of the few players to have started a [[Super Bowl]] with three teams: [[Super Bowl XXIX]] with the [[San Diego Chargers]], [[Super Bowl XXXIII]] with the [[Denver Broncos]] and [[Super Bowl XXXV]] with the Ravens.

He was the chaplain for the [[Chicago Bears]] before becoming the assistant player development director for the [[Baltimore Ravens]]. Harry and his wife Dawn have five children.

'''Harold Lucious McLinton''' (July 1, 1947 – October 31, 1980) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for the [[Washington Redskins]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1969 to 1978. He played [[college football]] for the [[Southern Jaguars football|Southern Jaguars]].

McLinton was selected by the Redskins in the sixth round of the [[1969 NFL/AFL draft]].  He spent his entire 10-year career with the Redskins, playing in 127 games.  He was a key contributor on the 1972 [[National Football Conference|NFC]] championship team.  He finished his career with four [[interception]]s and one [[touchdown]].

McLinton died on October 31, 1980, at the age of 33 from complications resulting from massive injuries sustained after being struck by a passing vehicle on [[Interstate 295 (District of Columbia)|Interstate 295]] in southeast Washington after stopping to help a stranger change a flat tire.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1992/12/10/inner-drive-to-excel-puts-terps-mclinton-on-road-to-frustration/ |title=Inner drive to excel puts Terps' McLinton on road to frustration |newspaper=Baltimore Sun |date=December 10, 1992 }}</ref>  He was a 1966 graduate of Harper High School in Atlanta, GA and went on to attend Southern on a football scholarship.  He graduated May 1969 with a bachelor's degree in Marketing & Management.

'''Harry Kent Newsome Jr.''' (born January 25, 1963) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Punter (football)|punter]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

Newsome was born in [[Cheraw, South Carolina]] and played scholastically at [[Cheraw High School]].<ref name="PFR1">{{Cite web |title=Harry Newsome Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/N/NewsHa20.htm |access-date=May 11, 2024 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He played collegiately at [[Wake Forest Demon Deacons football|Wake Forest]], and was a third-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] as a junior.<ref name="PFR1" /><ref name="Ithaca Journal">{{Cite news |date=Dec 6, 1983 |title=Associated Press All-American Team |work=The Ithaca Journal}}</ref>

Newsome was selected by the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] in the eighth round of the [[1985 NFL draft]].<ref name="PFR2">{{Cite web |title=1985 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1985/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-05 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He spent five years with the Steelers, followed by four years with the [[Minnesota Vikings]].

Harry holds the record for the longest punt in Three Rivers Stadium of 84 yards. He shares with [[Herman Weaver]] the [[List of NFL individual records#Punts had blocked|NFL record for most of his own punts blocked]] in a career with 14. In 1988, he set the NFL record for most of his own punts blocked in a season with 6.<ref name="Loede2013">{{cite book|last=Loede|first=Matt|title=100 Things Steelers Fans Should Know & Do Before They Die|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=caNuAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA42-IA2|accessdate=6 October 2016|year=2013|publisher=Triumph Books|isbn=9781623683016|page=42}}</ref>

Today, Newsome lives in his hometown, Cheraw, SC with his wife, Beth. Together, they have three children: Josh, Laurin, and Cody. After retirement, Newsome founded his own landscaping company.
